title: Three leads, no answer
spec: M02 · a chunker cuts a call chain, and nothing warns you
intro: Index orderflow, ask a structural question, and read what comes back. The retrieval succeeds by its own definition and the answer is still wrong — that is the whole lesson, and no better embedding model touches it.

provenance.source: a replayed retrieval session over labs/sample-project. The chunk boundaries in steps 1–2 are reproducible from the module's own chunker; the similarity scores and token counts in steps 3–5 are the module's LEADS_VS_ANSWERS figures. Steps 1, 2 and 6 carry their own citations.

foot: Make it fail on your machine: labs/M02-rag-shreds-context/README.md · the canonical-lookup half is labs/M06-okf-authoring/

steps.title: Index the repo the standard way
narrative: Nothing exotic here — this is the pipeline everyone builds. Walk every .py and .md file, split on paragraph boundaries into pieces of at most 400 characters, keep {text, source, chunk_index}, embed each piece, store the vectors.

Forty-six chunks out of fourteen Python modules and four Markdown files. Phase 1 is done. Notice what the pipeline never asked and never recorded: how any chunk relates to any other chunk. It stores distances, and distance is all it will ever know.
steps.youDo: cd labs/M02-rag-shreds-context and write the chunker — paragraph-aligned, 400 characters. Run it over ../sample-project/ and print the count.

steps.title: Where the chunker cut the call chain
narrative: orderflow's auth chain is three links long: post_invoice calls verify_token, which calls decode_jwt. Now look at where the 400-character boundaries landed.

The import from shared.auth import AuthError, verify_token is the last line of chunk #11. The call site claims = verify_token(authorization) is in chunk #12. The chunker cut between a symbol's import and its use — the two halves of the same fact, in two different vectors.

And verify_token's definition isn't in either of them; it is chunk #39, in a different file. As the module puts it: if cause and effect aren't co-located in the same chunk, your system has no idea they're connected. Here they are three chunks apart, and one of the cuts fell between adjacent lines of the same function.
steps.youDo: Open services/billing/app.py at lines 11 and 19, then shared/auth.py at line 41. Three links, two files, and your chunker put all three in separate pieces.

steps.title: Ask it a structural question
narrative: Phase 2. The question is the one an agent asks constantly before it dares change anything: who calls verify_token?

The query gets embedded, the index returns its three nearest neighbours, and every one of them scores high. Read the scores and then read what they mean: 0.89 says this chunk's language resembles your question's language. Not one of the three claims to contain a call.

steps.title: Read the shreds
narrative: Open them. Lead 1 is the top hit and it is the definition — def verify_token, the callee, structurally the opposite of what was asked. It scored highest precisely because it repeats the query's words most densely.

Lead 2 is webhooks.py, which handles tokens of a different kind entirely and never touches auth. Lead 3 is app.py — the right file — but the retrieved chunk is #11, the imports. It proves verify_token was imported; it does not contain the call.

The chunk that actually holds claims = verify_token(authorization) is #12, and it lost. Most of its 290 characters are a decorator, a signature and an exception handler; it says the query's words once. The one chunk with the answer ranked below three chunks without it — because ranking by similarity is not ranking by truth.
steps.claudeSays: Three chunks arrive with identical confidence tone and no structural claim attached. Nothing in the payload distinguishes the definition from a call site from an import.

after.title: WHY A BETTER EMBEDDER MAKES THIS WORSE

view.text: A perfect embedding model would represent each shred's meaning perfectly — and chunk #11 genuinely is about verify_token, so a better model ranks it higher, not lower. The information you need is the relationship between chunks, and it was destroyed at chunking time, before any vector was computed. There is no model upgrade that restores it, which is why the fix in this course is architectural rather than a shopping decision.

steps.title: The answer is confidently incomplete
narrative: The model receives three high-similarity chunks about authentication and does the reasonable thing: it answers. "verify_token is used by the billing service's request path and by webhook handling." Half true, unsourced, and unfalsifiable from what it was given.

Nothing crashed. No score dipped below a threshold. No log line said "the relevant chunk did not make the cut." This is the module's signature failure mode — silent wrongness — and it is the reason this walkthrough stops at the failure instead of rushing to the fix.

The agent's only recourse is the M00 tax: open each lead and read enough code to judge it. Three files, roughly 7,900 tokens, and at the end of it you have verified three leads and still cannot prove there is no fourth caller somewhere you never retrieved.

steps.title: The contrast — and the part where RAG still wins
narrative: Same question, different machine. A structural graph was asked to store this relationship at extraction time, so answering is a lookup: one call, one caller, a provenance tag attached. Fifteen tokens against 7,900, and only one of the two answers can tell you whether it is a fact or a guess.

Now the honest half, because deleting your vector database would be trading one over-correction for another. RAG was built to find relevant passages in a huge pile of unstructured text nobody will ever curate — years of Slack, a lake of one-off design docs, millions of tickets. On that corpus, with exploratory questions, similarity is exactly the right criterion and a graph has nothing to offer.

The professional default is RAG first, graph when depth becomes a bottleneck. Roughly 72% of enterprise RAG deployments underdelivered in year one — and the dominant causes were bad chunking, stale indexes and mismatched embedding models, not the absence of a graph. Adding a graph to a broken pipeline gives you a broken pipeline with higher operational overhead.
steps.youDo: Write down the two failure signatures that justify adding a layer: multi-hop structural questions failing, and canonical facts coming back stale or conflicting. Add nothing until you have observed one.
